title: Intersections & Being Seen
summary: How to handle intersections, parked cars and night riding, and how to make sure other drivers notice you.

blocks.text: The greatest potential for conflict between you and other traffic is at intersections. An intersection is anywhere traffic may cross your path, from a city crossroad to a driveway on a residential street.

items: Over one-half of motorcycle/car crashes happen because a driver violates the rider's right-of-way.
The biggest dangers are cars turning left in front of you (including from the lane on your right) and cars on side streets pulling into your lane.

blocks.text: Never count on eye contact. Drivers often look right at a rider and still fail to see them. The only eyes you can count on are your own: if a car can enter your path, assume it will.
Ride with your headlight on, choose a lane position with the best view of oncoming traffic, and keep a space cushion that leaves you an escape path. When a driver is getting ready to cross your path:

items: Slow down and pick a lane position that makes you more visible to that driver.
Cover the clutch lever and both brakes to cut your reaction time.
As you enter the intersection, move away from the vehicle, but do not change speed or position sharply. The driver may think you are about to turn.
Be ready to brake hard and hold your position if an oncoming vehicle turns in front of you, especially with other traffic around you.

blocks.text: Use this same strategy any time an oncoming vehicle is signaling a left turn, even in the middle of a block.

At a blind intersection, move to the part of the lane that brings you into the other driver's view as early as possible. For example, if a parked car on your right blocks the view of the cross street, ride in the left portion of the lane, away from the parked car.

items: If there is a stop sign or stop line, stop there first.
Edge forward and stop again, just short of where the cross-traffic lane meets your lane.
Lean your body forward and look around buildings, parked cars or bushes for oncoming traffic.
Keep your front wheel out of the cross lane while you look.

rows: Passing parked cars
Stay toward the left of your lane to avoid opening doors, drivers getting out and people stepping out between cars.
Parked cars plus oncoming traffic
The center of your lane is usually best, to keep space on both sides.
Car pulling away from the curb
The driver may not look, or may look and not see you. Slow down or change lanes to make room.
Car making a sudden U-turn
It can block the whole road. Slow down, get the driver's attention with your horn, and continue with caution.
Parking at a curb
Park at an angle with your rear wheel to the curb, unless a local ordinance requires parking parallel to it.

blocks.text: After crashes, drivers often say they never saw the motorcycle. A motorcycle looks small, and most drivers are not looking for one. Even when a driver does see you, smaller vehicles seem farther away than they are, so drivers pull out thinking they have plenty of time.
Pretend you are invisible. If you assume no one can see you, you ride more alert and notice more of what is around you.

items: Most crashes happen in daylight, so wear bright clothing. Your body is half of what drivers can see of you and your bike.
Bright orange, red, yellow or green jackets or vests are your best bets. Any bright color beats drab or dark colors.
A brightly colored helmet also helps others see you.

Reflective, bright-colored clothing (helmet and jacket or vest) is best. Reflective material on your vest and on the sides of your helmet helps drivers coming from the side spot you, and also helps drivers ahead and behind.
Keep your headlight on at all times. During the day, a motorcycle with its headlight on is twice as likely to be noticed.
Use your low beam in fog.
Signal every time you change lanes or turn, even when no one seems to be around or your plan seems obvious. Signal lights also make you easier to spot.
Entering a freeway, a blinking signal helps drivers coming from behind see you and make room.
Turn the signal off after you turn, or a driver may pull into your path thinking you are turning again.

blocks.text: A motorcycle's brake light is less noticeable than a car's. Flash it before you slow, especially when:

items: You will slow more quickly than others expect, such as turning off a high-speed road.
You will slow where others may not expect it, such as mid-block or at an alley.
You are stopped at an intersection with traffic coming up behind you.
Someone is following you closely. The tailgater may be watching you and not the hazard ahead.

blocks.text: Give a quick tap of the horn before passing anyone who might move into your lane:

items: A driver in the next lane crowding the car ahead and likely to pass.
A parked car with someone in the driver's seat.
A person in the street, walking or riding a bicycle.

blocks.text: In an emergency, sound the horn loud and long and be ready to stop or swerve. A motorcycle horn is not as loud as a car's, so use it but do not rely on it alone. You still need time and space to maneuver.
Check your mirrors often, and make a special point of it:

items: When you are stopped at an intersection. A driver coming up behind who is not paying attention could be on top of you before they see you.
Before you change lanes, to make sure no one is about to pass you.
Before you slow down, since the driver behind may not expect it.

blocks.text: Most motorcycles have rounded (convex) mirrors. They show a wider view than flat mirrors, but make cars look farther away than they really are. Practice judging distance with them, and still allow extra room before changing lanes.

Mirrors are not enough. Motorcycles have blind spots too. Before changing lanes, turn your head and look. On a road with several lanes, check both the lane next to you and the far lane, since a driver there may be heading for the same space.
At night it is harder to see and to be seen. To make up for it:

rows: Reduce speed
Ride slower than in daylight, especially on roads you do not know.
Increase distance
Distances are harder to judge, so keep three seconds or more behind, and allow more room to pass and be passed.
Use the car ahead
Its headlights can show the road better than your high beam, and its taillights bouncing up and down warn you of bumps or rough pavement.
Use your high beam
Whenever you are not following or meeting a car.
Be visible
Wear reflective materials.
Do not override your headlight
Ride slowly enough that you can stop within the distance your light shows you.
Be flexible about lane position
Move to the part of the lane that best helps you see, be seen and keep a space cushion.

keyPoints: Intersections hold the greatest potential for conflict; over half of motorcycle/car crashes are caused by a driver violating the rider's right-of-way.
Never trust eye contact: if a car can enter your path, assume it will.
Approaching a driver who may cross your path, slow, get visible, cover the clutch and both brakes, and avoid sudden changes in speed or position.
At a blind intersection, stop at the line, then edge forward and stop again with your front wheel out of the cross lane.
Wear bright, reflective gear and keep your headlight on at all times; drivers often think a motorcycle is farther away than it really is.
Signal every lane change and turn, cancel signals afterward, and flash your brake light before slowing.
Check mirrors often and always turn your head before changing lanes; convex mirrors make cars look farther away.
At night, slow down, keep 3 or more seconds of distance, use your high beam when no car is ahead or oncoming, and never override your headlight.
